sources.title: Nyambe Sumbwa, Traditionalism, Democracy and Political Participation: The Case of Western Province, Zambia (2000)
sources.note: Original University of Zambia research, African Study Monographs 21(3), pages 105 to 146; full PDF read. Historical sections pages 107 to 111 support institutions and colonial transformation. Modern survey includes interviews, archival and historical sources. Does not adopt the author’s broad idealization of precolonial democracy.

sources.title: Mutumba M. Bull, Lewanika’s Achievement (1972)
sources.note: Original historical study, Journal of African History 13(3), pages 463 to 472. Directly read published extract and detailed references, especially note 7 on dual administration. Actual publication 1972, not digitization 2009.

sources.title: Walima T. Kalusa, The Kololo Kingdom in the Upper Zambezi (2023)
sources.note: Oxford Research Encyclopedia chapter, published 18 October 2023; complete indexed abstract read, direct page failed. Abstract gives conquest 1838 whereas Sumbwa places it in the 1840s; public narrative uses broad mid-century phase rather than pretending exact agreement. Restoration 1864 and language influence concur.

sources.title: Zambia National Heritage Conservation Commission, The Barotse Cultural Landscape (2009)
sources.note: Official state heritage submission to UNESCO Tentative List, dated 10 March 2009, directly read. Not an inscribed World Heritage property or independent UNESCO endorsement. Sections Description and Traditions, techniques and management systems support mounds, canals, fishing and seasonal migration.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Lidded basket, Lozi artist, 2021.225a,b
sources.note: Primary museum object record directly read. Dated approximately 1900 to 1920, makenge root fiber and pigment, 16 by 31 by 62 centimeters. Curatorial discussion supports women’s weaving, storage, expansion under Lewanika and designs for outside clients.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of African Art, Lidded dish, 2019-8-6
sources.note: Primary object record, full indexed text read. Catalog attributes maker to King Lewanika and Lozi artist; late nineteenth to early twentieth century. Object description supports two antelope figures. Provenance uncertainty not converted into certain transfer dates.

sources.title: Matthew A. Cobb, Barbarians and Blemmyes: who was in control of the Red Sea port of Berenike in the Late Antique period?
sources.note: Original historical analysis, accepted manuscript directly read via repository PDF. PDF pages 13 to 16 discuss confederation, royal letters and limits of ethnic attribution; pages 23 to 27 discuss late antique power and competing models of port control. Do not flatten alternative models into exclusive sovereignty.

sources.title: Hélène Cuvigny and colleagues, Blemmyes: New Documents and New Perspectives (2022)
sources.note: Primary edition of excavated documents; publisher’s complete bilingual synopsis and table of contents read. Chapters IV and V concern Bi’r Samut and Xeron Pelagos. Gallienus reign, not erroneous 364 CE in some retailer summaries. The full paid book was not accessed.

sources.title: Rodney Ast, Szymon Popławski and Joanna Rądkowska, A Building Inscription for the Blemmyan King Kabantia (2022)
sources.note: Original publication of inscription, Chiron 52, published online 2023. Publisher abstract directly read; PDF access failed. Only abstract-supported discovery, royal name, location and broad fifth-century date used.

sources.title: Helmut Satzinger, The Papyrus Letter of the Blemmyan King Phonên
sources.note: Scholar’s translation of primary Greek letter, directly read. Identifies SB XIV 11957 = FHN III 319 and Skeat 1977/Rea 1979 editions. Uncertain pronouns and disputed reconstruction of military sequence are avoided. Fifth-century date corroborated by Cobb.

sources.title: Hans Barnard, Additional Remarks on Blemmyes, Beja and Eastern Desert Ware (2008)
sources.note: Author-posted complete original study read, Ägypten und Levante 17, pages 23 to 32. Pages 23 to 24 describe ceramics and 27 to 29 reject automatic attribution of all regional pottery to Blemmyes or equation of ancient and modern identities.

sources.title: Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona, Roman Empire’s Emerald Mines May Have Ended in Hands of Nomads (2022)
sources.note: Research team’s 1 March 2022 account of its 2020 and 2021 fieldwork, read in full. Fourth to sixth-century excavations, Tripartite Building and topographic survey. Mine galleries accumulated across working history; not all cut by identified Blemmyan workers.

sources.title: Joan Oller Guzmán and colleagues, A Falcon Shrine at the Port of Berenike (2022)
sources.note: Full author-posted excavation report read, American Journal of Archaeology 126(4), pages 567 to 591, DOI 10.1086/720806. Greek transcription and English translation read in stele section; no reconstructed missing letters. Shrine late-antique context does not establish exact carving date of reused stone.

sources.title: Santana and colleagues, The chronology of the human colonization of the Canary Islands (2024)
sources.note: Primary radiocarbon modelling, DOI 10.1073/pnas.2302924121. Indexed full article and PDF results read; direct PMC retrieval challenged. Models differ: broad first to fourth centuries CE, single-phase model 295 to 340 CE. Do not turn model limits into an exact founding date.

sources.title: Morales and colleagues, Agriculture and crop dispersal in the Canary Islands (online 2023; volume 2026)
sources.note: Full primary archaeobotanical study read. Introduction restricts Guanche properly to Tenerife; abstract lists crops; Gran Canaria results and discussion describe figs in dental cavities, whole dried figs in granaries and differing crop preservation.

sources.title: MUNA, Arqueología de Tenerife: exhibition and archaeological collections
sources.note: Full institutional exhibition account read: economy, bone and obsidian tools, repaired leather from funerary caves, and settlement examples Los Cabezazos and Ifara. Roof materials at Ifara are conjectural and omitted.

sources.title: José Juan Jiménez González, Los menceyatos guanches (Museos de Tenerife, 2014)
sources.note: Museum archaeological curator explains ethnohistorical accounts of territorial leadership, disputes and redistribution. Nine territories belong to late preconquest Tenerife, not the whole archipelago or its entire history.

sources.title: UNESCO, Risco Caído and the Sacred Mountains of Gran Canaria Cultural Landscape
sources.note: Official property account, description and authenticity: cave dwellings, granaries, cisterns, sanctuaries and Libyco-Berber inscriptions. Broad ancient-settlement date is superseded here by 2024 chronology. No unverified inscription translation or exact astronomical calendar asserted.

sources.title: Tabares de Nava and Santana Rodríguez, Testamentos de guanches, 1505 to 1550 (2017)
sources.note: Primary notarial texts edited from archives. Document 11, printed pages 37 to 38 (PDF pages 38 to 39), Juan Azanos, 18 November 1510, AHPT Protocolos Notariales 3, folios 471r to 472r. Exact Spanish excerpt and named interpreters verified. This is colonial Spanish recorded for a Guanche speaker, not Guanche language or Indigenous rock-script decipherment.

sources.title: Jesús Duque Arimany, Un ámbito, un panel y nueve menceyatos (Museos de Tenerife)
sources.note: Museum archival research account: conquest in 1496, dissolution of political territories, continued Indigenous participation, land allocations and surviving place names. Avoids repeating unsupported genealogies or treating all former rulers as having the same fate.

batchIdentityNotes.note: Imported 1783 to 1914 polygon follows the upper Zambezi floodplain, not every historically claimed tributary territory. Beginning is coverage, not founding. Kololo conquest chronology differs among the scholarly sources, so no exact conquest year is imposed. Restoration 1864 supported. Colonial authority developed through successive agreements, not a single fall in 1914. The modern 2009 landscape account is explicitly dated where describing household engineering, and objects spanning 1900 to 1920 are not artificially confined to map end.

Decoded Eastern Desert polygon, but 500 BCE to 800 CE is imported coverage rather than a single documented state. Period century boundaries are explicitly circa. Blemmyes, early Beja and modern Beja are not automatically treated as identical; no card sharing with bega or beja-people. Berenike was cosmopolitan and the degree of Blemmyan political control remains debated, so no universal attribution of all inhabitants or objects. Grain-voucher recipients are called Barbaroi in their documents. Writing is Greek within a relevant shrine, not claimed as a surviving Blemmyan vernacular sentence.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Shared phased account for two imported broad cultural labels covering the same Canary Islands outline. Guanche strictly identifies Tenerife; other island examples are explicitly named. Neither map interval is treated as a historical lifespan.
batchIdentityNotes.geometry: Both decoded bounds approximately -17.34 to -13.42 longitude and 27.73 to 29.43 latitude. First interval -1500 to 500, second 800 to 1878. Settlement, conquest and continuity warnings appear publicly.
batchIdentityNotes.writing: Actual Spanish notarial wording from a Guanche speaker through interpreters, 1510. Indigenous Libyco-Berber inscriptions acknowledged separately without an invented translation. The disputed late-attested term mencey is not offered as a securely reconstructed ancient-language sample.
